newsitem.title: FRANCE: Bulgaria flagged Hernu as agent - French ex-spymaster.
newsitem.headline: Bulgaria flagged Hernu as agent - French ex-spymaster.

text.p: Bulgarian secret services told France four years ago that the late Socialist ex-defence minister Charles Hernu had been a communist agent early in his career, a French former spymaster said on Wednesday.
Jacques Fournet, then chief of DST counter-intelligence, told France 3 television he could not check the report, but passed it on to then president Francois Mitterrand.
He said Mitterrand decided to classify the report as state secret, since Hernu who served as defence minister in 1981-85, had died in 1990 and could not defend himself from the charges.
"DST was not able to verify what was in this report...We can regard this file as somewhat suspicious," Fournet said.
The weekly L'Express earlier quoted secret files as showing that Hernu, a friend of Mitterrand's, had spied for the Soviet Union and other communist countries in the 1950s and 1960s.
Biographer Jean Guisnel said Hernu was too junior to know anything worthwhile at the time. The files did not say if he kept working for the east after he became defence minister.

Le Monde said that, based on spying reports reaching the West after the collapse of communism, British services in 1993 handed French authorities a list of 300 French foreign affairs officials alleged to have spied for eastern European countries.
There was no immediate comment on Le Monde report.

L'Express said Hernu was recruited as a rising political star by a Bulgarian spy in Paris in 1953, and was paid by Bulgaria, Romania and the Soviet Union for at least a decade for supplying reports about French politics.
It compared the Hernu case to the espionage scandals of British spy Kim Philby and Germany's Gunther Guillaume.
"I'm stunned, I knew nothing about this, like all the French people," Hernu's cabinet colleague Jacques Delors, finance minister from 1981 to 1984, told Europe-1 radio.

Asked whether the charges rang true, he answered: "For the moment, no, given what I know of him...We should find out if (his alleged reports) were reports on Paris establishment circles, or state secrets."
Former spy barons also urged authorities to shed light on what if anything Hernu allegedly supplied his Communist patrons.

"I've no idea whether this is true or false. Hernu was anti-Soviet and anti-Communist, but on questions (of spying) there is a complete break between public and private life," Pierre Marion, former head of the DGSE secret service, which answers to the Defence Ministry, told Reuters.
"These accusations are too serious not to be cleared up," he said.
Yves Bonnet, DST head in 1982-85, said Hernu may have been approached by east bloc agents early in his career but this should not overshadow later periods of his life.

"In managing the defence ministry, Hernu showed each time that it was necessary the greatest firmness not only towards the Soviet Union but also towards the head of the (French) Communist Party (Georges Marchais)," Bonnet said.
Patrice Hernu, one of the late minister's sons, urged President Jacques Chirac to shed light on the affair and branded the report "a fabrication coarsely sown together".

L'Express quoted the files as saying Hernu was known by the codenames of "Andre" or "Dinu" and had been paid monthly sums of several thousand francs (hundreds of dollars) for his work, including portraits of politicians like Mitterrand.
It said he accepted the equivalent of 300,000 francs ($60,000) in 1958 to fund an election campaign to parliament. but lost despite the cash.
Guisnel said Hernu's debts and rocky private life made him a wonderful quarry for manipulators. "But I await evidence," he said.

Hernu resigned in disgrace from the defence ministry in 1985 after French agents sank the Greenpeace ship Rainbow Warrior in Auckland harbour, New Zealand, as the vessel was preparing to protest against French nuclear testing in the South Pacific.
